newsitem.title: JAPAN: Manila seeks more talks with Beijing on Spratlys.
newsitem.headline: Manila seeks more talks with Beijing on Spratlys.

text.p: Philippine Foreign Minister Domingo Siazon said on Friday he looked to continue talks with China over the disputed Spratly Islands, the cause of a recent diplomatic row between Manila and Beijing.
"The very objective of our continued dialogue (with China) is to make sure we don't have to use warships," Siazon told an international conference on Asia's future, held in Tokyo.
Siazon said the dispute over the Spratlys, a cluster of reefs and islets in the South China Sea believed to hold oil deposits, must also be taken up in regional forums.
"The South China Sea is one of the region's most immediate problems over which we must maintain the pace of bilateral and multilateral dialogue," he said.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
He said it was important that most countries in the region were signatories to the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, which provides a legal framework to resolve such disputes.

Last week, China protested against the hoisting of a Philippine flag over a contested rock called Scarborough Shoal, also in the South China Sea but not part of the Spratlys, and accused Philippine naval ships of disrupting activities in the area by Chinese amateur radio groups.
The Philippines last month protested against what it said was the incursion of Chinese armed vessels into areas claimed by Manila in the Spratly Islands.
China, which says the Spratlys and all other islands in the South China Sea historically belong to the country, said the ships were Bureau of Fisheries vessels engaged in scientific research.
At the Tokyo conference, Siazon said regional concern over nuclear safety could also affect the Spratlys dispute.
"Should regional public opinion turn decisively against nuclear energy...this could intensify our region's growing dependence on oil and gas imports," he said.
"Dependence on (oil) imports may exacerbate rivalry over the region's offshore hyudrocarbon fuel resources, large concentrations of which are believed to exist in the South China Sea," he said.
